subtype: Approach: asking for the whole amount as a birthday gift [Thinking]
passage: Hrithik, you want to ask everyone for money this Diwali instead of presents? Your Jatin Chacha had the same idea once. I was eleven and wanted a clockwork train set, far more than my pocket money. I thought: Diwali is two months away, all the relatives come, everyone gives something. If I ask for money instead of sweets and shirts, I might get the whole train in one night. But then I thought, what if Bade Mamaji doesn't come? What if they forget? So I kept saving my coins every week anyway. Good thing. Mamaji's train from Kanpur was cancelled that year. The Diwali money came up short, and my own savings filled the gap.

qa.q: Why didn't Bade Mamaji come that Diwali?
qa.a: Mamaji's train from Kanpur was cancelled.

qa.q: What was young Jatin worried about after planning to ask for Diwali money?
qa.a: He was worried the relatives might not come or might forget, so he felt unsure about relying only on others.

qa.q: What choice in the story turned out to matter most?
qa.a: Keeping up his weekly saving as a back-up, because the Diwali money fell short and his own coins filled the gap.

qa.q: How might the relatives have seen being asked for money instead of gifts?
qa.a: They might find it a clear request, though it put part of the plan in their hands, as Mamaji's cancelled train showed.

grounding: Shows a boy planning to ask relatives for Diwali money instead of gifts, a shortcut that depends on others, so he keeps saving just in case.

subtype: Approach: asking for the whole amount as a birthday gift [Thinking]
passage: The science kit in the shop window had a sign: 'Only 3 left'. Harish had saved a little, but nowhere near enough, and Diwali was two months off. At dinner he thought out loud to his sister Rashmi. "At Diwali, Nani, Mama and Bua all give presents. If I ask them for money instead, I could buy the kit straight away." Rashmi raised an eyebrow. "And if they forget? Or the kit sells out?" Harish chewed his roti. "Then... I keep saving anyway. My own money plus whatever comes." So every Sunday his coins still went into the steel box. At Diwali two envelopes came, not three. Together with his box, it was just enough.

qa.q: What did the sign on the science kit say?
qa.a: 'Only 3 left'.

qa.q: Why did Harish chew his roti before answering Rashmi?
qa.a: Her questions made him unsure and a little worried about depending on others, so he stopped to think.

qa.q: What made Harish's plan safe as well as quick?
qa.a: He kept saving every Sunday, so when only two envelopes came, his own box covered the rest.

qa.q: How does Rashmi seem to see his idea?
qa.a: Rashmi raises an eyebrow and asks what happens if they forget, so she seems doubtful and practical about relying on relatives.

grounding: Illustrates a boy deciding to ask relatives for Diwali money, a quick route that relies on others, so he keeps saving as a back-up.

subtype: Approach: giving up when the goal seems too far [Pitfall]
passage:
"Didi, I've saved for two weeks and I've only got a hundred rupees."
"And the drone is six hundred?"
"Six hundred! It'll take forever." Arnab shook the tin. "The shop near the bus stop has a plastic helicopter for eighty. It lights up."
"You said you wanted the drone."
"I want something now."
Two days later:
"Didi... the propeller fell off."
Ishita looked at the helicopter on the floor, its light flickering. "Already?"
"And now the light's stopped." Arnab turned the tin upside down. Twenty rupees fell out. "I've got less than when I started."
"Want to start again?"
He looked at the twenty rupees for a long time.

qa.q: How much did the plastic helicopter cost?
qa.a: Eighty rupees.

qa.q: How did Arnab feel when the tin showed twenty rupees?
qa.a: He felt disappointed and regretful, with less than when he started and a broken toy.

qa.q: What could have helped Arnab when the goal felt too far?
qa.a: A smaller first target, or counting the weeks left with a parent; buying something now emptied the tin for a toy that broke.

qa.q: How does Ishita seem to see Arnab's choice?
qa.a: Ishita reminded him he wanted the drone and, after it broke, gently asks if he wants to start again, so she seems patient and kind.

grounding: Shows a boy who, after two weeks, feels six hundred rupees will take forever, spends his savings on a cheap toy that breaks, and ends up with less.

subtype: Approach: giving up when the goal seems too far [Pitfall]
passage: In Class 4 I was saving for a Rs 600 football, the real leather kind. After two weeks I had Rs 120, and I remember thinking: at this speed, I'll be in Class 5 before I get it. It felt like forever. So one evening, when Samir and I passed the fair, I spent all of it on a plastic car with flashing wheels. It was great for exactly three days. Then one wheel snapped, and the flashing stopped. I remember holding it and feeling stupid. I'd had Rs 120 and a plan; now I had a broken car and nothing in my tin. Samir said, 'Bhupen, you should've waited.' He was right.

qa.q: How much had Bhupen saved after two weeks?
qa.a: Bhupen had Rs 120.

qa.q: How did Bhupen feel holding the broken car?
qa.a: Bhupen felt stupid and regretful, having swapped a plan and Rs 120 for a broken toy.

qa.q: What could Bhupen have tried when Rs 600 felt so far away?
qa.a: A smaller first target, like Rs 200, or asking a parent to help plan the weeks, instead of spending everything at the fair.

qa.q: How does Samir see what happened?
qa.a: Samir thinks Bhupen should have waited, and says so plainly.

grounding: Illustrates a boy giving up on a Rs 600 goal after two weeks, spending his savings on a cheap toy that breaks within days, and ending up with less.

subtype: Approach: setting a smaller first target [Revision]
passage: When I was saving for the Rs 800 skateboard, there was a week when I just wanted to quit. I'd been putting coins in my box for a month, and it still felt like I hadn't moved. I noticed I was grumpy every time I looked at the box. So I changed the plan. Instead of 800, I wrote a new number on a sticker: 200. First stop. When I reached it three weeks later, my sister Binita shouted, 'Hrithik bhaiya, jalebi party!' and we had one jalebi each. Then I wrote 400 on a new sticker. It felt so much closer. By the end of term I had the skateboard, and Binita still reminds me about the jalebi party.

qa.q: What number did Hrithik write on the first sticker?
How did Hrithik feel before changing the plan?
qa.a: Hrithik felt discouraged and grumpy, as if a month of saving hadn't moved him closer.

qa.q: Why did the smaller target help?
qa.a: Reaching Rs 200 gave him a win to celebrate, which rebuilt his patience for the next step toward Rs 800 😊

qa.q: How does Binita remember the change?
qa.a: Binita still reminds him about the jalebi party, so for her it was a happy, fun moment.

grounding: Shows a boy noticing he feels discouraged, setting a first target of Rs 200, celebrating it, and carrying on toward the full price.

subtype: Approach: setting a smaller first target [Revision]
passage: Class teacher's note, 6A savings project, week 5. Harish came to me looking flat. He is saving for a Rs 1,000 telescope and said, 'It's never going to happen. I've only got Rs 150.' He had noticed himself that he was losing interest. I asked what might help. After a while he said, 'Maybe I stop looking at 1,000.' He drew a new line on his chart at Rs 200. Last Friday he reached it and the class clapped, which he loved. He has now drawn the next line at 400. Farida, who sits beside him, has split her own goal into steps too.

qa.q: What is Harish saving for?
qa.a: A Rs 1,000 telescope.

qa.q: How did Harish feel when he came to the teacher?
qa.a: He looked flat and discouraged, sure the telescope was never going to happen.

qa.q: What helped Harish, and whose idea was it?
qa.a: His own idea to stop looking at 1,000 and aim for Rs 200 first; reaching it and being clapped for rebuilt his patience.

qa.q: How does Farida respond to Harish's approach?
qa.a: Farida, beside him, has split her own goal into steps too, so she seems to find the idea useful.

grounding: Illustrates a boy who notices he is discouraged, sets a smaller first target of Rs 200, celebrates reaching it, and keeps going.

subtype: Approach: changing her mind after thinking again about the want [Revision]
passage:
Saturday
Six weeks of saving for the robot dog that barks and does a flip. Today I held my tin and thought: after the first week, will I still play with it? Hemant bhaiya's robot car has been under his bed, dusty, since Holi. I tried to picture next month: me, and the robot dog sitting on the shelf. Then I looked at my other shelf. The mystery books I love, and my old broken crayons. I'd read a new book series again and again. I'd draw every day. So I've changed my mind. The money is going to the five-book mystery set and a proper art box. Maa said, 'Gargi beti, that's a grown-up choice.' I feel light.

qa.q: Where has Hemant's robot car been since Holi?
qa.a: Under his bed, dusty.

qa.q: How does Gargi feel after changing her mind?
qa.a: Gargi feels relieved and sure, having chosen things she'll use every day.

qa.q: What question helped Gargi decide, and why is it useful?
qa.a: Whether she'd still play with the toy after a month; picturing next month showed which choice would last.

qa.q: How might Maa see Gargi's choice?
qa.a: Maa calls it a grown-up choice, so she seems proud of how Gargi thought it through.

grounding: Shows a girl who, after six weeks of saving, asks whether she'll still play with the toy in a month and chooses books and an art set instead.

subtype: Approach: changing her mind after thinking again about the want [Revision]
passage: For six weeks Gargi had saved her coins in a clay pot, all for the wind-up toy train at the stall near the bus stand. On the evening of the Dussehra mela she walked there with her brother Vaibhav, the money knotted in her dupatta. The train went round its little track, bright red. Gargi watched it, then remembered Vaibhav's spinning top from last year, lost in the cowshed within a month. Would she still play with the train after the mela? She looked at the next stall: a set of four Hindi storybooks and a box of wax crayons. She'd read those till the pages went soft. "Books and crayons," she said. Vaibhav stared. "Not the train?" Gargi shook her head, already choosing the first book.

qa.q: Where had Gargi saved her coins?
qa.a: In a clay pot.

qa.q: What was Gargi thinking as she watched the train?
qa.a: She felt unsure, remembering Vaibhav's lost spinning top, and wondered whether she'd still play with the train after the mela.

qa.q: Why was thinking again before spending a wise step?
qa.a: It helped her pick books and crayons she'd use for a long time, instead of a toy she might forget within a month.

qa.q: How does Vaibhav see Gargi's choice?
qa.a: Vaibhav stares and asks 'Not the train?', so he's surprised she changed her mind.

grounding: Illustrates a girl who has saved for weeks rethinking whether she'll still want the toy in a month, and choosing storybooks and crayons.

subtype: Approach: breaking cleaning his room into small jobs [Thinking]
passage: Note for Dhruv's parents, Saturday, from Dadi. This morning Dhruv stood at his door and said, 'It's too much, I can't.' His room was a jungle. I said nothing and waited. After a while he sat on the bed and began thinking out loud. 'Clothes first. Only clothes.' He put every shirt and sock into the basket or the cupboard. Then, 'Now books.' Then toys into the box. Last, the floor, with the jhadu. Each time he finished a part he said, 'That's done,' and looked a little taller. Samir came to borrow a ball and said the room looked new. It took an hour. I've told Dhruv I'm proud of him.

qa.q: What did Dhruv tidy first?
qa.a: Clothes first, only clothes.

qa.q: How did Dhruv feel standing at his door at first?
qa.a: He felt overwhelmed, saying 'It's too much, I can't.'

qa.q: What made the room manageable for Dhruv?
qa.a: Splitting it into clothes, books, toys and floor and doing one at a time, so each finished part made the rest seem smaller.

qa.q: How does Samir see the room afterwards?
qa.a: Samir says the room looks new, so he is surprised and impressed.

grounding: Shows a boy overwhelmed by a messy room splitting it into clothes, books, toys and floor and doing one part at a time.

subtype: Approach: breaking cleaning his room into small jobs [Thinking]
passage:
Sunday evening
Mummy said the room had to be clean before Nani's visit tomorrow. I opened the door and wanted to shut it again. Clothes on the chair, books under the bed, building blocks everywhere, dust. I thought, if I look at all of it at once, I'll never start. So I wrote a list on my hand in pen: CLOTHES, BOOKS, TOYS, FLOOR. Just clothes first. That took ten minutes. I crossed it out. Books, fifteen. Toys, the worst, twenty. Floor, easy. Kashish, my little sister, came in at the end and said, 'Siddharth bhaiya, where's all your stuff?' It's all where it belongs! My hand is covered in ink, but I did it.

qa.q: Where did Siddharth write his list?
qa.a: On his hand, in pen.

qa.q: How did Siddharth feel when he first opened the door?
qa.a: Siddharth felt overwhelmed and wanted to shut the door again.

qa.q: Why did the list on his hand help?
qa.a: It turned one huge mess into four small jobs, and crossing each out showed him progress.

qa.q: How does Kashish react to the clean room?
qa.a: Kashish asks where all his stuff has gone, so she seems surprised by how tidy it is.

grounding: Illustrates a boy overwhelmed by his messy room splitting it into clothes, books, toys and floor, and finishing one part at a time.

subtype: Approach: putting everything on the bed then sorting it [Action]
passage:
"Himani, your floor is invisible."
"I know. Help me?"
"Where do we even start?"
"Everything on the bed. All of it."
They scooped: jeans, a hairbrush, three library books, a sock with a hole, sweet wrappers, a broken bangle.
"Now what?"
"Three piles. Cupboard, shelf, bin."
"Jeans?"
"Cupboard."
"Library books?"
"Shelf. Oh! I thought I'd lost that one. It's due Monday."
"Broken bangle?"
Himani paused. "Bin."
"Sock with a hole?"
"...Bin."
Twenty minutes later the bed was empty and the floor was actually tiles. Ayesha flopped down. "It's like a different room."
"It's like I can think in here," said Himani.

qa.q: What three piles did Himani make?
qa.a: Cupboard, shelf and bin.

qa.q: How did Himani feel on finding the library book?
qa.a: Himani felt relieved and surprised, having thought it was lost, with it due on Monday.

qa.q: Why did putting everything on the bed help Himani choose?
qa.a: Seeing it all in one pile showed exactly what was there, so Himani could send each thing straight to cupboard, shelf or bin.

qa.q: How does Ayesha see the room at the end?
qa.a: Ayesha flops down and says it's like a different room, so Ayesha is pleased with their work.

grounding: Shows a girl piling everything from the floor onto the bed and sorting it into cupboard, shelf and bin, which makes each choice easier.

subtype: Approach: putting everything on the bed then sorting it [Action]
passage: Last summer my room got so messy that I stopped even seeing it. Then my cousin Sabina came to stay and asked, 'Charu, where do I sleep?' That was the moment. I tried picking things up one by one, but I kept getting distracted. So I did something drastic: I put everything from the floor on the bed. Everything. Clothes, crayons, a lost earring, old test papers, a dried-up pen. The heap was taller than my pillow. Then I sorted: cupboard, shelf, bin. Seeing it all together made the decisions easy; I didn't need four old tests. By dinner the floor was clear, and there was room for Sabina's mattress.

qa.q: What made Charu finally start tidying?
qa.a: Cousin Sabina came to stay and asked, 'Charu, where do I sleep?'

qa.q: How did Charu feel trying to pick things up one by one?
qa.a: Charu felt distracted and stuck, so that way wasn't working.

qa.q: What made the sorting easier once everything was on the bed?
qa.a: Seeing it all in one heap showed what was there, so choices like binning four old tests became easy.

qa.q: How did the tidying change things for Sabina?
qa.a: Sabina finally had space for a mattress on the cleared floor.

grounding: Illustrates a girl moving everything from the floor onto the bed and sorting it into cupboard, shelf and bin, which shows what is there and eases choices.

subtype: Approach: stuffing things under the bed to look clean [Pitfall]
passage: I share a room with my brother Gurpreet, so I saw the whole trick. Mummy said, 'Clean your side in five minutes or no cricket.' Gurpreet looked at the mess, then at the bed. In went everything: socks, comics, his school shoes, a half-eaten biscuit packet, all shoved underneath with his foot. Mummy peeped in and smiled. 'Very good!' He went off to cricket, grinning. Next morning at 7:15, the van was honking and Gurpreet was flat on the floor, arm under the bed up to the shoulder, pulling out socks and comics but no shoes. I don't know what he was feeling, but he looked like he wanted to cry.

qa.q: What did Gurpreet shove under the bed?
qa.a: Socks, comics, his school shoes and a half-eaten biscuit packet.

qa.q: What might Gurpreet have been feeling as the van honked?
qa.a: He looked close to tears, so he probably felt panicky and sorry he'd hidden the shoes.

qa.q: What would have worked better than hiding the mess?
qa.a: Putting things in their places, even quickly, like shoes by the door; hiding them made the room look neat but lost the shoes.

qa.q: How does Mummy see the room the day before?
qa.a: Mummy peeps in, sees a neat room and says 'Very good!', not knowing the mess is under the bed.

grounding: Shows a boy hiding clutter under the bed to satisfy his mother quickly, then being unable to find his school shoes the next morning.

subtype: Approach: stuffing things under the bed to look clean [Pitfall]
passage:
Saturday. Guests were coming, and Mummy said, 'Kunal, your room, ten minutes.' Kunal pushed everything under the bed: clothes, cards, his school shoes, a cricket pad. Mummy looked in. 'Wah, so neat!' Kunal felt pleased with himself.
Sunday. His cousin Zeenat rolled a marble under the bed and reached in after it. Out came a sock, a comb and a smell. 'Kunal! It's a jungle under here!'
Monday. At 7:20, with the van outside, Kunal lay flat pulling out cards and clothes, hunting for his school shoes. He found one. The van left. The other turned up ten minutes later behind the cricket pad, and Mummy had to take him to school herself.

qa.q: Where was the second shoe?
qa.a: Behind the cricket pad.

qa.q: How did Kunal feel on Saturday when Mummy praised the room?
qa.a: He felt pleased with himself, since the room looked neat so quickly.

qa.q: What would you change first in Kunal's cleaning?
qa.a: Put things where they belong, starting with school shoes by the door; hiding everything turned Monday morning into a scramble.

qa.q: How does Zeenat see what's under the bed?
qa.a: Zeenat is shocked and calls it a jungle, so she sees the mess the neat room was hiding.

grounding: Illustrates a boy stuffing clutter under the bed to please his mother, leaving the mess in place and his school shoes lost on a school morning.

subtype: Approach: racing the clock to make it a game [Thinking]
passage:
Tuesday
I hate tidying my desk. So today I tried a trick. I set the kitchen timer for ten minutes and said, 'Beat yesterday.' Yesterday it took me fourteen minutes of moaning. Today I made it a race: pens in the jar, books stacked big to small, papers in the tray, crumbs in the bin. I was so busy watching the timer that I forgot to be bored. Eight minutes, forty seconds! Aai said, 'Chaitanya beta, are you feeling well?' Tenzin phoned and I told him my time. He says he'll race me tomorrow with his room. Game on.

qa.q: How long did tidying take yesterday?
qa.a: Fourteen minutes of moaning.

qa.q: Why did Chaitanya forget to be bored?
qa.a: He was so focused and excited about beating the timer that the chore felt like a game 🎉

qa.q: What could keep the race fun after a few days?
qa.a: Racing Tenzin, or setting a new target, so there's always something to beat; the race is what keeps his attention on the job.

qa.q: How does Aai react to the tidy desk?
qa.a: Aai jokes 'are you feeling well?', so she seems surprised and amused by the quick tidying.

grounding: Shows a boy setting a ten-minute timer to beat yesterday's time, turning a boring chore into a race that holds his attention.

subtype: Approach: racing the clock to make it a game [Thinking]
passage: Every evening Pranav had to sweep the courtyard of their village house, and every evening it took forever, because he kept stopping to watch the goats. On Wednesday he had an idea. If it's a race, I won't have time to be bored. 'Vaibhav, watch the clock. Ten minutes. Yesterday it was fifteen. I'm going to beat it.' Vaibhav squatted by the old wall clock. Pranav swept like a cyclone: neem leaves into one pile, dust out through the gate, the corner behind the water drum last. He didn't look at the goats once. 'Nine minutes!' Vaibhav shouted. Pranav leaned on the broom, panting and grinning. 'Tomorrow, eight.'

qa.q: Where did Vaibhav squat to keep time?
qa.a: By the old wall clock.

qa.q: How did Pranav feel when Vaibhav shouted 'Nine minutes!'?
qa.a: He was panting and grinning, so he felt proud and excited to have beaten yesterday's time.

qa.q: What else could Pranav race against?
qa.a: His own best time each day, or Vaibhav on another chore; the race keeps his attention off the goats.

qa.q: What is the race like for Vaibhav?
qa.a: Vaibhav gets the job of timekeeper and shouts the result, so he seems to enjoy being part of it.

grounding: Illustrates a boy turning sweeping into a race against a ten-minute target to beat the day before, which keeps his attention on the chore.

subtype: Approach: making a chore chart with turns among siblings [Action]
passage: When Mummy's leg went into plaster, the flat fell apart in two days. Plates piled up, the tulsi drooped, and Jyoti, Urmila and their little brother Raju were fighting about who did what. 'I watered the plants yesterday!' 'I laid the table twice!' Jyoti took a chart paper and drew three columns: laying the table, watering the plants, sweeping. Down the side, Monday to Sunday. Then she wrote their names across, shifting one box each day, so the jobs rotated. She stuck it on the fridge. Mummy read it from the sofa and laughed. On Thursday, when Raju groaned about sweeping, Urmila just tapped the chart. Raju picked up the broom.

qa.q: What happened to Mummy?
qa.a: Mummy's leg went into plaster.

qa.q: How did Raju seem to feel about sweeping on Thursday?
qa.a: He groaned, so he felt reluctant, but he accepted it when Urmila tapped the chart.

qa.q: Why did rotating the names help stop the fights?
qa.a: Everyone could see the turns change each day, so nobody could claim to be doing more than the others.

qa.q: How does Mummy see the chart?
qa.a: Mummy reads it from the sofa and laughs, so she seems relieved and amused that the children sorted it out themselves.

grounding: Shows three siblings making a chore chart with rotating names for laying the table, watering plants and sweeping, so nobody feels they do more.

subtype: Approach: making a chore chart with turns among siblings [Action]
passage: In their Dehradun flat, every evening ended the same way: 'Why do I always lay the table?' 'You never water the plants!' Chetan, the eldest of the three, finally got out a sheet of chart paper and sat his sisters Nidhi and Gauri at the table. They listed the jobs: lay the table, water the balcony plants, sweep the hall. Then Chetan drew a grid for the week and wrote their names in turns, moving along one each day. 'Monday I lay, Nidhi waters, Gauri sweeps. Tuesday, we shift.' Gauri checked it twice to make sure it was fair. Their neighbour Tenzin, visiting on Saturday, saw it on the fridge and asked if he could copy it for his house.

qa.q: Which city is their flat in?
qa.a: Dehradun.

qa.q: Why did Gauri check the chart twice?
qa.a: She wanted to be sure it was fair, probably worried she'd been doing more than her share.

qa.q: What else could make the chart work well?
qa.a: A swap rule for busy days, agreed by all three; open, rotating turns are what stop anyone feeling they do more.

qa.q: How does Tenzin see the chart?
qa.a: Tenzin likes it enough to ask if he can copy it for his own house.

grounding: Illustrates three siblings writing chores on a chart with names rotating each day, so the turns are open and nobody feels they do more.

subtype: Approach: complaining and delaying until asked five times [Pitfall]
passage: 'Astrid, can you fold the laundry?' 'Later, Pappa.' Twenty minutes passed. 'Astrid, laundry.' 'In a minute!' Her sister Clara folded her own pile and went back to her book. A third time, a fourth. By the fifth time, Pappa was standing in the doorway of their Oslo flat, arms crossed. 'Now, please.' 'Why do I always have to do everything?' Astrid shouted. It became an argument, voices rising, a door slammed. In the end she folded the laundry anyway. It took twelve minutes, exactly what it would have taken the first time. But it was now seven o'clock, her cartoon had already finished, and Pappa said the TV stayed off tonight.

qa.q: How long did folding the laundry take?
qa.a: Twelve minutes.

qa.q: How did Astrid feel when she shouted 'Why do I always have to do everything?'
qa.a: She felt frustrated and resentful, though the argument only made things worse.

qa.q: What would have saved Astrid her cartoon?
qa.a: Folding the laundry the first time Pappa asked; it took twelve minutes either way, but delaying added an argument and cost the cartoon.

qa.q: How did the evening feel for Pappa?
qa.a: Pappa asked five times and ended up arms crossed in the doorway in an argument, so he was likely tired and annoyed.

grounding: Shows a girl putting off a chore each time her father asks, until it becomes an argument and she loses her evening cartoon.

subtype: Approach: complaining and delaying until asked five times [Pitfall]
passage: Vinita's father was the caretaker at the community centre, and after the evening yoga class her job was stacking the forty plastic chairs. 'Vinita, chairs,' he called. 'Later, Papa, I'm talking to Pooja.' Five minutes. 'Vinita, chairs.' 'Coming!' She didn't come. A third call, a fourth. By the fifth, Papa's voice was sharp, and Vinita snapped back, 'Why can't someone else do it?' They argued right there in the hall, while Pooja stared at the floor and slipped away. In the end Vinita stacked the chairs. It took fifteen minutes, like always. But by the time they walked home, her favourite cartoon was over, and Papa said nothing all the way.

qa.q: How many plastic chairs did Vinita stack?
qa.a: Forty plastic chairs.

qa.q: How did Vinita feel when she snapped back at Papa?
qa.a: Vinita felt annoyed and resentful at being called again, which turned the delay into an argument.

qa.q: What could Vinita do differently next evening?
qa.a: Stack the chairs at the first call and talk with Pooja afterwards; delaying still took fifteen minutes and added an argument and a missed cartoon.

qa.q: What was the argument like for Pooja?
qa.a: Pooja stared at the floor and slipped away, so Pooja seemed uncomfortable and embarrassed.

grounding: Illustrates a girl delaying a chore through five calls from her father until it turns into an argument and costs her evening cartoon.
